title: Fit wisp to count data — wisp
code: # A tiny synthetic count-data set with one obvious transition point: two # spatial blocks of 10 bins each, with Poisson-process counts at rates 2 and 8. set.seed(1) n_bins <- 20 bin <- sample(seq_len(n_bins), 400, replace = TRUE) lambda <- rep(c(2, 8), each = n_bins / 2) countdata <- data.frame(bin = bin, count = rpois(400, lambda[bin]))  # fit_only = TRUE skips MCMC/bootstrap resampling, so this fits in well under # a second; see sample_stats() for estimating parameter uncertainty. model <- wisp(   countdata,   fit_only       = TRUE,   model.settings = list(LRO_cost = "none"),   plot.settings  = list(print.plots = FALSE),   verbose        = FALSE ) model$fitted.parameters #>     baseline_context_Rt_species_Tns/Blk1  #>                                 3.890853  #>     baseline_context_Rt_species_Tns/Blk2  #>                                 5.061927  #> baseline_context_tslope_species_Tns/Blk1  #>                                 7.494465  #> baseline_context_tpoint_species_Tns/Blk1  #>                                10.699851   # The two rate ("Rt") parameters above (about 3.89 and 5.06) don't look like the # true rates of 2 and 8 used to simulate the data. That's because wisp fits the # log transform (plus one) of the *summed* count within each bin, not the # per-row rate itself. To recover the original rates, exponentiate the fitted # rate, subtract one, and divide by the mean number of data rows per bin within # that block (see the "Poisson processes and sigmoids" tutorial for the full # explanation): tokens_per_bin <- tabulate(countdata$bin, nbins = n_bins) for (block in 1:2) {   bins           <- (block - 1) * 10 + seq_len(10)   mean_tokens    <- mean(tokens_per_bin[bins])   rate_param     <- model$fitted.parameters[block]   recovered_rate <- (exp(rate_param) - 1) / mean_tokens   cat("Block", block, "recovered rate:", round(recovered_rate, 3), "\n") } #> Block 1 recovered rate: 2.294  #> Block 2 recovered rate: 8.214
